title: Query Projection — 7 Learning Questions
subtitle: Topic: Query Vector Generation and Attention Computation · Subject: Transformers and LLM Architecture. Three beginner, two medium, two advanced questions with accessible diagrams and simple explanations.
hero:
QUERY PROJECTION · VISUAL MAP

Teach each token what to search for

A learned projection produces a Query for each token. Attention compares it against Key vectors to choose which information to combine.

questions.stem: What is Query Projection in Transformer models, and how does it transform a token's representation into a Query vector that helps the model determine which other tokens are relevant?
options: A learned map makes each token a Query vector for comparison with other token Keys.
Query Projection stores whole sentences in a fixed table to retrieve matching texts during language generation.
Query Projection selects the next word directly, without comparing attention scores against any token Keys.
Query Projection first turns text into pictures so attention can detect relevant features across images.
questions.explanation: In simple words: Query Projection turns token features into search vectors. Attention compares them with Keys to find which other tokens are relevant.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: A. Query Projection is a trainable linear mapping applied to a token’s current hidden-state representation. A Query is a numerical vector representing what a token can match against other tokens’ Keys. Standard Transformer self-attention computes Q=XW_Q and K=XW_K, then uses scaled dot products between them to form attention scores. A separate learned Query mapping gives the model flexibility beyond comparing the original embeddings directly.

A token is turned into a vector for searching context

Remember: Query Projection learns a new view of the token's features, which attention uses to compare against Keys.

questions.stem: What is the difference between Query, Key, and Value projections in Self-Attention, and why does a Transformer need a separate Query representation instead of using the original token embedding directly to calculate attention?
options: Queries carry information to return, Keys predict answers, and Values decide which token positions to inspect.
All three projections make identical vectors, so separate learned matrices cannot influence attention behavior.
Queries express what to match, Keys represent possible matches, and Values carry the information to combine.
Only Values have trainable weights, while Query and Key projections always copy input embeddings unchanged.
questions.explanation: In simple words: Queries look for matches, Keys offer matches, and Values carry information. Separate learned projections make these roles more flexible.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: C. Query, Key, and Value have separate learned projection matrices: Q=XW_Q, K=XW_K, and V=XW_V. Query/Key similarity gives attention scores and Softmax turns scores into weights, which combine Values. Query and Key focus on matching; Value contains features to aggregate. Direct embedding comparisons are possible in other designs but lose the standard model’s separate learned matching and content roles.
questions.figure:
02 · LEARNING DIAGRAM

Query finds matches; Key qualifies them; Value carries content

Remember: The separate matrices W_Q, W_K, and W_V learn different representations of the same hidden states.

questions.stem: How does Query Projection work when processing the sentence "The cat sat on the mat," starting with token embeddings, applying a learned weight matrix, generating Query vectors, and comparing those Queries with Key vectors to determine attention scores?
options: Each token's Query is stored as a word label; attention then ranks labels alphabetically without weights.
Each token's Query comes from projection; comparison with Keys gives relevance scores across the sentence.
The Query for cat always attends to the nearest word, regardless of learned weights or context.
Queries are computed after Softmax, so attention probabilities determine them before any similarity calculations happen.
questions.explanation: In simple words: Each sentence token gets a Query. Comparing the Query for “sat” with other Keys produces attention scores.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: B. In the sentence The cat sat on the mat, token embeddings or hidden states form X. Learned matrices produce Q and K. To compute attention for sat, compare q_sat with each of the six Key vectors. For the diagram's illustrative scores [0.1,1.8,0.2,0,0.1,0.4], Softmax gives [9.2%,50.5%,10.2%,8.4%,9.2%,12.5%]. Real models may produce different weights depending on their projections, positional encodings, attention masks, and learned parameters.

questions.stem: How does the mathematical equation \(Q = XW_Q\) describe Query Projection, and how do the input hidden dimensions, learned projection weights, output dimensions, and matrix multiplication determine the resulting Query vectors?
options: Projection weights multiply learned word counts into IDs, so matrix shapes cannot affect the resulting Query output at all.
Query matrix dimensions determine original batch size, while input sequence length fixes the number of attention heads.
Every Query copies its input embedding exactly, so learned projection weights cannot change the final feature width.
X[T,8] times W_Q[8,4] yields Q[T,4], preserving tokens but changing feature size.
questions.explanation: In simple words: A learned weight matrix changes how many Query features each token has, while preserving the number of tokens.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: D. Using row vectors without bias, the projection is Q=XW_Q. For X of shape [T,d_model] and W_Q of shape [d_model,d_q], Q has shape [T,d_q]. The inner dimensions must agree. For X=[[1,2,0],[2,0,1]] and W_Q=[[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]], the output is Q=[[1,2],[3,1]]. The token dimension T stays unchanged. A PyTorch nn.Linear layer stores weight dimensions transposed internally and can add an optional bias.
questions.figure:
04 · LEARNING DIAGRAM

The Query weight matrix changes feature width—not token count

Remember: The matching inner dimension makes multiplication valid. The output preserves the number of token rows.

Standard rule: Q = XW_Q, with X∈ℝT×d_model, W_Q∈ℝd_model×d_q, Q∈ℝT×d_q. A Linear layer may add a bias.

questions.stem: How can Query Projection be implemented using Python and PyTorch, including creating a linear projection layer, transforming batched token embeddings into Query tensors, reshaping them for multiple Attention Heads, and examining the resulting tensor dimensions?
options: Use nn.Linear to project token vectors; reshape and transpose split the resulting Queries into distinct heads.
Create plain Python lists of token IDs per head and run word loops without learned matrices.
Apply torch.softmax to raw token IDs before making Queries or splitting the embedding tensor across heads.
Reshape original token embeddings into separate heads before projection, then permanently fix all Query weights to zero.
questions.explanation: In simple words: PyTorch Linear makes Query features. Reshape and transpose organize those numbers into multiple attention heads without changing their values.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: A. In PyTorch, nn.Linear(d_model,H*d_head) maps each token to concatenated Query head features. With B=2, T=6, d_model=8, H=2, and d_head=4, x has shape [2,6,8]. A linear projection preserves that example’s last-dimension width, returning [2,6,8]. Reshape to [2,6,2,4] and transpose axes 1 and 2 to obtain [2,2,6,4]. The code was tested locally using PyTorch. The learned projection changes values, but reshape/transpose change only the organization of those values.
questions.figure:
05 · LEARNING DIAGRAM

Learn one Query projection, then organize its output into heads

Remember: Each head receives four features per token. Query projections use learned weights, but reshape itself does not learn.

import torch
from torch import nn

B, T, d_model, heads = 2, 6, 8, 2
torch.manual_seed(7)
x = torch.randn(B, T, d_model)
Wq = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
q = Wq(x)                     # [2, 6, 8]
q = q.reshape(B, T, heads, 4)
q = q.transpose(1, 2)        # [2, 2, 6, 4]
print(q.shape)
Verified PyTorch output

torch.Size([2, 2, 6, 4])

Linear learns the features. Reshaping only organizes those values into heads.

questions.stem: How does Query Projection interact with Key Projection, Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), attention scaling, and the Softmax function inside Multi-Head Self-Attention, and how do these operations influence which tokens receive higher attention weights?
options: RoPE rotates Softmax probabilities only after attention, while Key and Query vectors never interact with one another.
RoPE rotates Query and Key vectors by position; scaling and Softmax then produce normalized attention weights.
RoPE removes learned Query weights entirely, and attention scaling multiplies logits by the full embedding dimension.
Softmax builds Keys and Queries from Values, then assigns token positions using their vocabulary IDs.
questions.explanation: In simple words: RoPE adds positional information to Queries and Keys. Scaled matching scores go through Softmax to produce attention strengths.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: B. RoPE rotates projected Queries and Keys in position-dependent feature subspaces. Attention scores come from the dot product of rotated Q and K, scaled by the square root of the head dimension, optionally masked, and then passed through Softmax. The resulting weights combine Value vectors. RoPE is not applied to Softmax probabilities. Some specialized architectures such as MLA decouple their positional path from low-rank KV content.
questions.figure:
06 · LEARNING DIAGRAM

RoPE changes Query–Key matching before the Softmax step

Remember: After projection, rotate Q and K, take their scaled similarities, apply any mask, and normalize with Softmax.

questions.stem: How does Query Projection behave in advanced Transformer architectures such as Multi-Head Attention (MHA), Multi-Query Attention (MQA), Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), and Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), and what trade-offs arise in projection dimensions, computational efficiency, KV-cache usage, and inference performance?
options: MHA shares one KV head; MQA has independent KV heads; GQA uses more cached heads than MHA.
Every attention variant caches Query vectors and recomputes all past Keys and Values for each new token.
MHA has per-head KV; MQA shares one; GQA shares groups; MLA compresses cached KV representations.
MLA removes KV compression altogether, keeping full Key and Value tensors for all Query heads.
questions.explanation: In simple words: MHA keeps separate Key/Value heads; MQA and GQA share heads. MLA compresses cached Key/Value information to save memory.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: C. MHA typically has independent Key and Value heads for each Query head; MQA uses one shared KV head; and GQA shares KV heads across groups of Queries. This reduces the size and memory bandwidth of an autoregressive KV cache. MLA compresses Key/Value information into a low-rank latent state, with a separate positional component in DeepSeek-V2; its Queries may also be compressed during training. Query heads still make attention lookups, while past K/V information is what is usually cached. Speed benefits depend on implementation and hardware.
questions.figure:
07 · LEARNING DIAGRAM

Attention variants mainly change how Keys and Values are cached

Remember: MHA keeps many KV heads, MQA shares one, GQA shares groups, and MLA compresses the cached KV representation.

Key difference: MHA uses separate KV heads; MQA shares one; GQA shares by groups; MLA stores compressed KV latents and a positional component. Reduced cache size can help inference but does not guarantee a faster end-to-end model.
